newsitem.title: JAPAN: Prosecutors enter DKB HQ in apparent raid -- Jiji.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors enter DKB HQ in apparent raid -- Jiji.

text.p: Prosecutors were seen entering the headquarters of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) on Tuesday in what appeared to be a raid, Jiji news agency reported.

A DKB spokesman said some officers from the Tokyo Prosecutors' Office had entered through the main reception area of the headquarters building, but they could not confirm whether the purpose was to raid the premises.

On Monday, DKB declined to comment on Japanese media reports that it was being questioned by prosecutors over its questionable loans to a racketeer at the centre of the Nomura Securities Co Ltd scandal.
It said it could not comment on its deals with individual customers.
The daily Mainichi Shimbun had reported that the bank had been questioned over its loans to "sokaiya" Ryuichi Koike, a principal figure in the Nomura scandal.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori Koike were arrested last Thursday on suspicion of violating Japan's Commercial Code by taking some 50 million yen in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a third senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
The Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.

On Monday, the Mainichi also reported that Ryuichi Koike owned about 20,000 DKB shares under various assumed names, and often attended DKB's annual shareholders' meeting as a "friendly sokaiya". Typically, "friendly sokaiya" uses their influence to stop "enemy sokaiya" from making extortion attempts at annual shareholders' meetings.
The DKB spokesman also declined to confirm on Monday whether Ryuichi Koike was a shareholder of the bank.

The Mainichi and other Japanese newspapers have also reported that DKB holds problem loans worth 7.5 billion yen linked to Koike, and also that another financial firm with close ties with DKB has Koike-linked bad loans worth 1.2 billion yen.
After the Nomura payoff scandal was revealed in early March, media reports said DKB loaned three billion yen in 1989 to a real estate company owned by the younger Koike.
The elder Koike reportedly used the money to buy 300,000 shares in each of the nation's top four brokerages including Nomura, and put up the shares as collateral for the DKB loans.
Shares in Dai-Ichi Kangyo slid in early Tokyo trading on Tuesday following media reports on the apparent raid.
As of 0011 GMT, the shares were down 60 yen at 1,410 yen, making the bank the biggest percentage loser on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange. Turnover was 1.13 million.
